sections.title: Introduction
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: About Me - Guide Last Updated: 2026-09-12
This is Aayrl's Beginner Guide to the Archer class in Monsters & Memories and is intended for players who wish to learn the basics of playing a ranged physical utility DPS class.
In this guide, I will assume you are playing to have fun. The goal here is to provide you with the basics to ensure you can be a successful solo archer or contributing member of a successful group.

sections.title: Race and Stats
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: Archers are a physical DPS class. As a result, you generally want to prioritize STR (increase damage dealt) and DEX (increase hit change) as your primary stats.

All races have a similar starting STR and DEX value. Ogre has the highest STR (22) combined with a decent DEX (19), followed closely by Goblin with STR (17) and DEX (23). Generally, DEX will be fulfilled by key pieces of gear later in the game, but damage is damage, so STR is generally the ideal stat to prioritize at character creation.

All races can use the bonus 10 points to reach the STR cap, so the race choice is a matter of personal preference in my opinion. I recommend choosing a race/body type that is smaller in size for hit box considerations later in this guide. Humans also have Tenacity as a utility racial ability that can help you in certain scenarios.

sections.title: Traits
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: See Traits for more information

sections.title: High Ground
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: The Archer class is unique in Monsters and Memories as being the only class with its own guaranteed free trait (as of 2026-09-12)!
The High Ground trait adds a 5% damage bonus when your attacks hit a mob that is on lower ground than you.

In practicality, this means you have a mild damage bonus when standing on a rock, crate, wall, hill, etc while fighting enemies. Keep this in mind as you play by simply reminding yourself that you are a Legolas/Obi-Wan hybrid.

sections.title: Major Combat
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: There are two really prominent options here in my mind:
Strong which gives you a permanent 5% STR boost as well as a 50% STR buff for 15 seconds every few minutes. This is handy to add some burst DPS to a named mob encounter or boss fight, or a bad pull.

Magic Resistant which gives you a permanent base +10 MR plus a 15% MR increase for any MR gear in the future. You also gain a utility ability to remove all harmful magic effects and increase resistance to them for 15 seconds. This is incredibly handy for mobs that Snare, Blind, Root, or Fear, since it gives you a get-out-of-jail-free card to recover from a bad pull or buy some time for your other group members to recover.
Any of the other resistance traits may have their uses depending on your goals, but I personally pick the Magic Resistant trait for added utility in group play.

sections.title: Major Noncombat
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: I generally pick Forage or Infra/Ultravision depending on race selection. Any option here is fine based on your character goals.
Fast Metabolism might be the min-max pick due to the mechanics of the High Ground class trait, but more testing is needed as my results so far are inconclusive (more on this in a bit..)

sections.title: Minor Combat
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: Bowman is the pick here and that should be obvious. You are an Archer, aren't you?
Bowman gives you a 25% skill increase to Archery as well as starting at Archery 5. You also gain a Trainee's Longbow, Trainee's Hip Quiver and 1000 Trainee's Arrow.

sections.title: Minor Noncombat
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: Fletcher is the preferred starting profession, but you can realistically pick any of these if you want.

Fletcher gives you a Trainee's Fletching Kit as well as a base level 25 Fletching skill (you can make Copper Arrow immediately) and a 5% skill rate increase for Fletching. You will be making a TON of arrows over the life of your character, and this will help you breeze past skill combines to the next tier of arrows along the way.

sections.title: Starting Location
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: Archers are diverse and as a result have fairly flexible starting location options.
Consider a starting location based on the starter quest rewards that match your desired play style.

Archer Starter Quest (Night Harbor) - Middle of the road option, any race can start here, close to the most developed major city hub for optimal grouping, vendor access, no ground breaking class quest rewards.

Archer Starter Quest (Faelindral) - Incredible early game Bow reward at around level 10 - Scout's Longbow of the Wyrdguard - Lasts well into your level 30s at the cost of limiting your race selection slightly.
Archer Starter Quest (Underdocks) - The evil option. Has some great group play opportunities and ties in nicely with the other class quests.
House Vael'xirith (Quest) (Ail'Vorith) - Unclear at time of writing. TBD.

sections.title: Tradeskills
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: Once you've loaded into the world and started working on your respective class quest, I recommend acquiring a few copper and buying the following tradeskills as soon as possible (in order):
Fletching (if you didn't pick the trait)
Lumberjacking
Mining
Smelting
You can train all the other tradeskills as you wish, but these four are quintessential to maintaining arrow supply for the Archer class.
Lumberjacking allows you to harvest wood, an essential requirement for Fletching.
Mining allows you to harvest ore, which can be smelted via Smelting and deconstructed into various scraps (also using Smelting) to make higher tier arrows later in the game.
As you level your character, always carry your Lumberjack Axe and Mining Pick to harvest nodes as you're exploring the world to maintain your supply of arrows.

You can leave your fletching supplies in a bank as your quiver will hold up to 10,000 arrows at a time, and you'll likely hit other limits forcing you back to town before you will need to make more arrows.

sections.title: Gear Upgrade Priority
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: The most impactful upgrades for your Archer will be:
Bow
Arrows
Gear with DEX for hit rating as needed (more on this later)
Gear with STR for damage
If you hit a wall with upgrades and are tight on cash, always prioritize the Bow upgrade as this will provide you with the biggest impact.
Focus on the highest DMG bow you can attain for your level as the DMG modifier applies to most of your abilities as well. ATK DELAY is important as well and we'll cover this a bit later.

sections.title: DEX versus STR
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: My general rule of thumb is if a piece of gear has STR or DEX and your previous piece of gear does not, that is an upgrade.

Once you hit the higher levels, STR becomes more important to hit the bigger damage numbers, and you will find sufficient DEX to maintain appropriate hit ratios for your level of enemies through jewelry or unique drops.

I have not performed enough testing since the Archer rebalance a few weeks ago, but the above information should still hold relatively true. I know there are ongoing adjustments to DEX calculations, so this is subject to change.

sections.title: Basic Combat
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: As an Archer, your auto attack will automatically swap between your Bow and Melee Weapon depending on how close the enemy is to you.
If you have played World of Warcraft as a Hunter, this will feel familiar to you. If you haven't, that's fine, you can say you have after trying Archer.
Archers are significantly more deadly with a Bow than with a melee weapon. In short, you want to keep your enemies at a distance as much as possible.
Next, let's go over a few techniques you'll need to practice to master the art of keeping your enemies at a distance.

sections.title: The Most Important Buff
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: As an Archer, your most important buff is Speed of the Wild, commonly referred to as "SoW".
Befriend as many Druids and Shamans as you can find, and always beg and plead when in town for a SoW.
This single buff will increase your damage output, kill speed, and utility more than any gear upgrade. Let's talk about why...

sections.title: Movement Keys
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: You will need to be comfortable strafing to be a successful Archer. There is no way around it, sorry.
If you enjoy the default keybindings and holding the Right Mouse Button all the time, that's great!
If you prefer to keybind strafe, hit ESC -> Settings -> Keybinds and map Strafe Left and Strafe Right to your A and D keys respectively.
Me? I use the default keybinds and the right mouse button. I find it easier to use the mouse to adjust my kiting with more sensitivity. Try both and see which method works for you.
You are strafing successfully if you can:
See the mob you are attacking
Your character is facing the mob you are attacking
You are running in an opposite direction from the mob you are attacking
You can see where your character is running towards

sections.title: Kiting
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: Kiting is the act of dealing damage to an enemy while constantly moving away from them to avoid any melee attacks.
At level 1, you start with Point Blank I and no movement speed buffs (unless a passing caster grants you Speed of the Wild, but more on this buff in a moment.)
Find a few mobs, stand as far away as possible, and begin auto attack. As the mob enters melee range, use your point blank attack, and then run away. Practice strafing here.
Keep running away and spam your Point Blank I ability. If you are successful, you should be just outside of melee range of the mob, but successfully firing off Point Blank I.

Remember character select? Hopefully you chose a slim character model, because the larger your character model is, the harder it is to stay out of melee range of a mob. While not impossible, some Ogre may find kiting as an Archer somewhat difficult.

At level 2, you can learn Barbed Arrow I (akin to Serpent Sting in WoW) which will deal 50% weapon ratio damage plus 2 bleed damage every 6 seconds for 18 seconds. Your rotation becomes pull with auto shot followed immediately by Barbed Arrow I. Start counting in your head to 18 seconds so you know when to reapply.

At level 3, you start to learn some utility with Disengagement. This allows you to jump backwards from your target every 20 seconds. Save this cooldown for when a mob is about to enter your melee zone and use it to stay at range.

At level 4 when you can learn Skirmisher. This ability is a self-aura that grants a 10% movement speed and 20% cooldown reduction buff permanently (until you die and have to recast it to apply). This makes kiting significantly easier as the small 10% movement bonus is enough to keep you perpetually out of melee range of most low level mobs.
At this point, you can start kiting in large circles. Practice this by starting with your auto shot and Barbed Arrow I, then start running in a small circle to keep the mob trailing behind.

As you continue to level up, you will gain more abilities that can add more damage while running mobs in a circle (I like to call this circling the drain). Quick Shot I becomes an instant damage ability to use in-between re-applying Barbed Arrow I. Snaring Shot can be used to keep mobs at a distance if they get too close in tandem with Disengagement (try to keep these on separate cooldowns, don't use them both at once.)

Strafing Barrage I opens up at level 8 which gives you a rapid fire multiple shot ability every few seconds. This makes kiting mobs faster and opens up your solo abilities to start taking on entire camps of mobs by yourself.
At this point, you've likely got a handle on the basics, so it's time to get into some more advanced tactics.

sections.title: Stutter Stepping
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: Stutter Stepping is exactly what it sounds like. Rather than simply running a giant circle around our mob, we're going to occasionally stop moving and take an auto shot at them. You'll start to understand why Speed of the Wild is so important here.

First, let's talk about your weapon ATK Delay. If you didn't already know this, your ATK Delay is the time between auto attacks. Divide the visible number by 10 to arrive at the number of real-time seconds between auto attacks. For a bow with an ATK Delay of 40, this equates to 4 seconds.
To successfully stutter step, you need to be good at counting out a number of seconds equivalent to your weapon's ATK Delay in your head constantly .
Let's elaborate on what this looks like in a combat scenario.
You target a mob and stand at maximum distance.
You toggle Q and engage combat by casting Auto Shot.
You cast Barbed Arrow I and begin moving away from the mob.
You start counting in your head .. 1 .. 2 .. 3 .. 4 .. and you stop moving
You stand still and watch your character cast Auto Shot.
You cast Quick Shot I and begin moving away from the mob.
What is going on here?
Auto shot can only be cast while your character is facing your target, and while your character is not moving.
When you were kiting, you were always moving, and therefore never firing auto shots. This reduces your total damage output tremendously.
By halting movement periodically and weaving in auto shots, your damage output increases exponentially.

Why are you counting to your weapon delay? When you fire your weapon, the ATK Delay is essentially a little timer that starts ticking down until another auto shot can be cast. You are counting down the timer so you can precisely stop moving for a half second to fire another auto shot before moving.
The more movement speed bonus you have (Skirmisher, Speed of the Wild), the easier it is to stutter step while keeping the mob at a distance.
Don't forget your other abilities as well if needed to stay at a distance - Disengagement, Snaring Shot, Caltrops, Immobilizing Trap, etc.
Once you are comfortable stutter stepping in a straight line, start practicing in circles.

As you gain confidence in killing single mobs this way, try pulling two, or three, or an entire camp. As long as you can run faster than the mobs, you can continuously chew down a full camp of mobs without taking any damage.
There is one major caveat here -- this assumes the mobs you are fighting aren't able to hit you with range or magic.
Do not practice on casters or range mobs. Practice strictly on melee mobs. Casters generally have a mana bar when you attack them, so really the only surprise should be range mobs.
Once you have mastered the basics of stutter stepping, there's one more key mechanic worth mentioning again...

sections.title: I Have the High Ground
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: Remember that innate ability we talked about above?
The High Ground trait adds a 5% damage bonus when your attacks hit a mob that is on lower ground than you.

Here's where things can get interesting. If you are playing in an open world zone, such as Sungreet Strand, then there are lots of locations where you can pull a camp of mobs and time your auto shots / abilities strategically when you are on an incline.

The goal is to find a slope or a hill (or a valley is ideal) to run your circle kites on. Every time your character is further up the hill than the mob you are killing, use your Jedi mind powers to remind yourself that you have the high ground and shoot the mob for that juicy 5% damage bonus.

Something that requires further testing - In theory, if your character is jumping, that would put them at a higher z-axis than the mob. So, in theory, would jumping before shooting on a flat surface grant the 5% damage bonus from the High Ground trait? My testing has been inconclusive so far, but I welcome anyone with evidence this is the case, as it would make the Fast Metabolism trait the most useful for Archers.
Alright, let's talk about leveling and play styles.

sections.title: Soloing
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: As a solo archer, the world is your oyster.
Prioritize finding large, open world locations with lots of room to kite and proximity to player hubs so you can continuously refresh your Speed of the Wild with your friendly neighborhood caster.

The best experience is generally found with camps of melee mobs that can be stutter-stepped in a circle. If you are successful, you should have no problem keeping a camp (or two) of blue-con mobs locked down.
If you are interested in high-stakes targets, such as named mobs, always leverage your utility abilities and plan an escape route if things go awry.
Try to keep your mobility cooldowns spread apart as best as possible to mitigate risk. A reminder on your utility cooldowns as a solo archer:
Disengagement - Lvl 3 - 20s Cooldown - Leap backwards from your target a short distance
Snaring Shot - Lvl 7 - 30s Cooldown - Slows your target by 50% for 6 seconds
Interrupting Shot - Lvl 8 - 16s Cooldown - Interrupts your target's casting - good to cancel a snare, blind, heal, etc.
Caltrops - Lvl 12 - 60s Cooldown - Enemies who stand in the caltrops have their speed reduced by 65%. Place this before you pull a camp.
Immobilizing Trap - Lvl 16 - 60s Cooldown - The first target that crosses the trap is rooted for 20 seconds.
Relocate - Lvl 26 - 120s Cooldown - 40% movement speed buff plus instant-invis for 4 seconds.
Anticipate - Lvl 30 - 900s Cooldown - 100% dodge chance for melee attacks for 15 seconds. Use this if you get rooted while pulling a camp.
Magic Resistant Trait - 300s Cooldown - Clears magic debuffs and high resistance for 15 seconds.
Tenacity - 300s Cooldown - HUMANS only - Remove Mez / Incapacitate effects, immune for 15 seconds.

sections.title: Group Play
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: There's several options to group play. I'll go over a few here based on my experience so far in Monsters and Memories, but there are likely other scenarios possible that I have not experienced myself and thus cannot provide guidance on.
E.g., at time of writing, I have not performed any raid content as an Archer, so if you are looking for Raiding expertise I cannot help you (yet).

sections.title: Duo
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: The best classes to duo with as an Archer are (hopefully unsurprisingly) a Shaman or Druid. Druid is preferred for the extra utility of teleporting for vendoring or finding new mobs to kill.
Have your caster friend maintain Speed of the Wild at all times and assist with using snares, roots, or heals to recover from any poorly executed pulls or kiting.
The healing from your Duo partner shouldn't be exhausting, as you shouldn't be getting hit very much and targeting outdoor camps.
If you are looking to find gear in a dungeon, it is in your best interest to find a larger group where possible. Duoing in small, indoor spaces is tough as an Archer.

sections.title: Big Group as a Ranged DPS
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: Find a group with, at minimum, a tank that can taunt and a healer. Movement speed is less critical here if the tank can successfully hold agro off of your bursty DPS, which opens up some new utilities to play with:
Sniper's Blind - Lvl 14 - Quick Shot damage booster.
Flurry of Arrows - Lvl 20 - Instantly resets the cooldown of most shots and increases your attack speed by 20% for 15 seconds and stacks with haste. Use this for named mobs or big pulls.

Marksman - Lvl 24 - This can replace your Skirmisher if you aren't kiting mobs in your group. Increases the damage of various shots and adds the ability to land CRITICAL HITS with your ranged attacks. Big damage.
Deadeye - Lvl 60 - 50% damage increase for 15 seconds.

Remember your training, Padawan. I have the high ground. Always seek a box, crate, stairway, bench, any object that physically puts your character at a higher Z-axis than the mob you are killing for that extra 5% damage bonus.
Don't forget your utility as an archer and your stutter-step training. If a pull goes sideways, your class can easily intercept with crowd controlling abilities
Caltrops - Lvl 12 - 60s Cooldown - Enemies who stand in the caltrops have their speed reduced by 65%. Place this behind your tank for your ranged DPS to kite mobs if they rip agro away from the tank.
Immobilizing Trap - Lvl 16 - 60s Cooldown - The first target that crosses the trap is rooted for 20 seconds. Place this near your healer or squishy caster DPS in case a mob breaks away from the tank.
Anticipate - Lvl 30 - 900s Cooldown - 100% dodge chance for melee attacks for 15 seconds. You can use this to face tank a melee mob and buy your healer some time to recover.
Or..as a last resort.. shooting mobs to make them angry with you and running in a big circle until your tank and healer can recover.

sections.title: Big Group as a Puller
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: If you are elected the group puller, hopefully you have Speed of the Wild in your group. You will want to keep Skirmisher up as well, but if you are feeling confident in your tank's abilities, you can toggle between Marksman when killing mobs in the kill zone between pulls.
Since you control the flow of mobs, you can also better leverage some of your utility abilities to pre-crowd-control a pull. A reminder on some tools at your disposal:
Caltrops - Lvl 12 - 60s Cooldown - Enemies who stand in the caltrops have their speed reduced by 65%. Place this before you pull a camp.
Immobilizing Trap - Lvl 16 - 60s Cooldown - The first target that crosses the trap is rooted for 20 seconds. Place this near your healer or squishy caster DPS in case a mob breaks loose.
Relocate - Lvl 26 - 120s Cooldown - 40% movement speed buff plus instant-invis for 4 seconds. Reset your pull if you mess up epicly.
Anticipate - Lvl 30 - 900s Cooldown - 100% dodge chance for melee attacks for 15 seconds. Use this if you get rooted while pulling a camp.

sections.title: Closing Remarks
sections.source: Aayrl's Beginner Archer Guide
lines: If you wish to learn more advanced techniques with the Archer class, I would recommend reviewing the Monsters and Memories Archer Forums and reviewing World of Warcraft Hunter Kiting videos, as the same skillset applies to Archers in Monsters and Memories.
Remember to play nicely in the open world. Just because you are an overpowered Archer who can solo camps of mobs doesn't mean you should grief other players.
You have the High Ground.

sections.title: Overview
sections.source: Bluing's Cleric Guide August 2024
lines: Clerics are fully functional healers.
The purpose of a healing cleric is to maintain alive the target of its heals (usually the tank of the group) through casting of spells, and resource management.

Casting healing spells costs mana. The best healing spells are those that cost the least amount of mana, for the most amount of healing in exchange, e.g. Impart Blessing (level 4 spell), costs 20 mana for a heal of 40 HP, with a 6 second delay; whereas Lesser Heal will instantly heal a target for 30 HP in exchange for 25 mana points. Finding the right use to each specific spell is also certainly useful, even though maybe out of the reach of this guide. To optimize your healing, you should always try to spend the least amount of mana in order to keep everyone alive. Prioritize the important targets in your party (including yourself) in essential in every situation. Dying yourself is just as dangerous, if not more, than letting a tank or another friend die (in party scenarios). Raid healing may vary a bit in terms of priority but is basically the same, except keeping the tank alive can potentially be more important than your own character in specific situations.

Another key point of healing is resource management. In M&M, to regain mana (at a reasonable rate), you must be sitting. Your character will then recover some mana every once in a while, and you will be able to keep casting spells. The essence of managing your mana as a cleric stems from never being full on mana if there are targets who need healing, and making sure you are sitting as much as possible to keep your mana regen up whenever possible. (For a more complex explanation on how mana regen works, and how to take advantage of it: The server ticks every 5-10 seconds. During this tick, many events go off (mana regen, stamina regen, etc,). Mana regeneration occurs every time this server tick happens. Every n seconds (between 5 and 10), if you are sitting whenever that happens, your character will recover some missing mana. Using this knowledge to maximize your uptime hitting your target, while sitting at key points to recover mana will make you a master at your class. Certain animations will synchronize with server ticks, making keeping track of them a lot easier, e.g. Bard songs, certain buffs, etc.). Knowing how to weave casting with sitting and hitting is what differentiates a bad from a good healer.

sections.title: A guide for a starting Elementalist (Valid as of May, 2026)
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: About the guide: This guide assumes that the player knows the common jargon of MMOs like EverQuest. This guide tries show how the Elementalist works and the how and why of playing the class. The spell list in the second section of the guide will be updated as possible.

sections.title: Why an Elementalist?
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: The Elementalist is a great starting main class. It is not a gear dependent class, though any Int and Mana gear helps out. A naked Elementalist with a pet is still DPS potent. They are an especially great class for farming tradeskill materials, particularly tailoring and leatherworking, and they can summon items that are useful to the Elementalist and other classes.
In combat, the pet does 90% of the DPS output of the Elementalist, with the Elementalist throwing in a few direct damage casts as needed. The pet DPS output is solid and reliable.
The Elementalist is frequently desired by groups looking for strong sustained DPS.
The Elementalist can summon helpful items for a group, themself, or pets; for example, bandages, food, drink, manastones, and weapons/ammo.

The only downsides are that the Elementalist has no specific crowd control ability, they can't heal anything except their own pet, and they can only add a few utility or resistance buffs and a damage shield to other players.

sections.title: Starting Races and Stats
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: Surprisingly, Ogres make very good Elementalists. They can start with 28 intelligence (add 8) and add the 2 remaining points into strength for 22 (helps with carry weight). Stamina is already good at 23 default. There is a drawback to playing as an Ogre; by default they are hated by the Wood Elves and are kill on sight. There areas in Keepers Bight with Wood Elves that must be avoided. Obviously the Wood Elf city of Faelindral is off limits. For the most part this is not a major problem, but it is something to be aware of.

Gnomes are a good choice because they can get 29 maximum starting intelligence and it only costs 5 starting points. However they will not have as good strength or stamina stats. The player can choose to go for a balance of Strength/Stamina stats or tip in one direction or the other.

Human and Dwarf Elementalists intelligence both start at 27 maximum for some reason, so they are both sub-par in this regard. A Dwarf is slightly better by point distribution options for strength and stamina after maxing intelligence, but only just. This doesn't mean that these races can't be twinked out to be better than Ogres or Gnomes, but they don't get the best starting stats.

All this said, ultimately the starting stats for the Elementalist don't matter all that much because the pet does all of the heavy lifting. The player can opt to ignore maxing Intelligence and go for some other balance of stats and it will not have a large impact on gameplay.

sections.title: Combat and Noncombat Traits
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: Intelligent is probably the best Combat Trait to pick for an Elementalist, although the 50% buff for 15 seconds is virtually combat useless. There may be a benefit in some way to tradeskills or other special circumstances.
For Minor Combat Trait, Channeler or one of the casting skills is fine.
For Major/Minor Noncombat Traits, it makes little difference, Master Artisan may be the best way to go for tradeskills and then some tradeskill like Tailoring.

sections.title: A few notes about Tradeskills:
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: If the player intends to do Jewelcrafting with the Elementalist or an Alt, it is highly recommended for the Elementalist to select the Disenchanter Minor Noncombat Trait. The reason is that disenchanting is required for components to enchant an item (such as rings, earrings, necklace, etc). Disenchanting is punitively difficult to level up from zero, requiring the destruction of many low level magic tagged items in order to successfully get components for use in Jewelcrafting. So starting out a skill level of 25 helps out quite a bit. An Alt, such as an Alt Enchanter, should choose Master Artisan and Jewelcrafting as the Major/Minor Noncombat skill. That said, all tradeskills can feel punitively difficult to level up from zero, but the more 'expensive' are the tradeskills like Disenchanting where it's necessary to regularly burn up magical items or mined Crystalized Magic shards.

As mentioned earlier, an Elementalist makes a spectacular collector of items for tradeskilling; good for mining, tailoring, leatherworking, lumberjacking, etc. After leveling up into the mid 20s and beyond, the Elementalist's pets are able to roll through various low level areas and mow down everything for components, such as gems, cloth, and rawhide scraps. Many of the outdoor areas where groups of enemies are located have nearby nodes for mining and lumberjacking.

Farming lower level named MOBs in dungeons or other areas for magic items to disenchant gets to be very easy (albeit tedious and time consuming waiting for respawns). For this, the dedicated pet classes (Elementalist, Beastmaster, and Necromancer) really shine because other classes usually have to be several levels higher or have difficulty due to their inherent limitations.

sections.title: Starting Out From Zero
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: The Elementalist will start out with two spell scrolls Flameburst and Minor Spellshield, scribe these to the spellbook and put the spell book on a belt slot in the character inventory.

If not twinked and the Elementalist has no money, kill enough starting mobs to loot items that can be sold to the butcher, or weapons/armor vendor if lucky with a skeleton drop. Be sure to visit a greedy gnome vendor in the starting area for the free bag. At about 100 copper or so, go get the spells Minor Creation: Air and Summon Minor Fire Staff. Also needed is Crushed Malachite (19 copper each currently), buy a few. The vendor for Crushed Malachite is the Elementalist Quartermaster, found in the Monk/Elementalist trainer area of Night Harbor. When there, start The Pinwheel Quest, as this results in a progressivly better belt with +INT/Mana for each stage completed.

Summon three staves (two for the pet and one for the Elementalist). Destroy the starting weapon after this, the summoned weapon is better. Summon the Air pet and hand in the two staves to it. The pet stays as long as it survives and it has not been dismissed. It will come back after a logoff and logon. The Air pet is the staple pet for a Elementalist. Generally, most Elementalists rely on this pet as it has the highest DPS of the four pets. Early on, the pets are not terribly durable, and the Elementalist has no way to heal them. Take care to not over-extend a fight and be sure to help the pet melee down targets.

The icons in the pet window are important to understand! There are three (four with Earth pet) icons with an animated outline (the animation means automatic activation by the pet). Right-click on an icon to deactivate the animated outline, which changes the ability manual. When the Elementalist clicks on the icon, it manually activates the pet's ability. Normally while in a group, the Elementalist should change the status of Provoke to manual. The others can be changed, but this only to control the ability, for example to manually activate the pet's damage ability so that the Elementalist can folow up with a Blast spell for a combo effect. Any time the icon is not greyed out (on cooldown), The Elementalist can left-click it and the pet will immediately use the ability (if possible). The idea behind turning off automatic use of Provoke is that in a group with a tank, the pet should not pull aggro off of the main tank. In a pinch, the Elementalist can manually trigger it if needed (for example off-tanking an add).

sections.title: The Air Pet
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: The Air pet Minor Creation: Air is recommended because it has the highest DPS, grants the group an aura buff (Rush of Air) that can add melee offhand/ranged bonus attacks (10% chance), and it has a stun ability Staggering Winds. the Air pet's Staggering Winds in combination with the Elementalist's Blast of Fire, causes a reaction spell conversion to Vortex of Fire, more on this below. In a group, two or more Elementalists with Air pets can chain stun a target so that the target barely has any time to do any damage. For most leveling, the Air pet is the Elementist's mainstay, especialy in the early levels up to 20 or so.

sections.title: The Water Pet
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: In second place, the Water pet Minor Creation: Water is just a little underneath the Air pet for overall DPS output. It's no slouch, the Water pet's DPS output is close to the Air pet and it has similar toughness to the Air pet. In a group that is heavy with casters, the Water pet's aura for mana regeneration (Fount of Mana) is hard to say no to. The Water pet's ability is Bolt of Water, essentially an ice bolt type of ranged attack. Presently there is no Elementalist blast combination with the pet's ability. If there is no Enchanter in the group, it might be a necessity to use the Water pet to avoid longer medding periods between pulls.

sections.title: The Earth Pet
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: Not widely used but sometimes needed, the Earth pet Minor Creation: Earth can be a main tank in a pinch, but the group will need a decent healer to or two to stay on top of healing the pet. It's aura, Earthen Toughness, buffs up the group's stamina and it has a special defense buff for itself (Earthen Skin). It's DPS output is not great, but it can be buffed up by the group to be a pretty tough tank. The Blast of Water spell reacts with the Earth pet's ability (Elemental Root) which creates a "mud slide"; this is a snare, handy to keep low health mobs from being able to flee away quickly.

sections.title: The Fire Pet
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: The least used (and pet with no compelling reason to ever buy or use) is the Fire pet Minor Creation: Fire. It would be generous to say that this pet is "niche". It's aura (Backlash of Fire) increases the group's casting speed and gives the group a damage shield. The Elementalist can cast a fire based damage shield on players or pets already, and the fire pet damage shield aura does stack with this, but it effectively adds 50% more damage shield damage. So a tank with the Elementalists' casted fire shield of 25 points will get a further 12 points from the fire pet's aura. The casting speed increase of XX% doesn't really matter and it is hard to fathom why the pet was designed this way. Even if casting time on a spell is cut by 50%, there is still the global cooldown and anyway burning up mana faster doesn't achieve much for the Elementalist or a typical group. The Fire pet's ability is Elemental Fire, which can react with the Elementalist's Blast of Water to create Cloud of Steam (a blind effect) on the target, or with Blast of Air to create Backdraft (a 20 meter knockback) on the target. Backdraft is generally not something to use solo or in a group without a clear reason, as it could create problems in tight quarters with adds.

sections.title: Spell Recommendations
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: Since the pet spells have to be purchased again every four levels, it simply isn't worth buying all of them unless money is no problem at all. Buying the Air and Water pets every four levels is recommended, with the Earth pet being somewhat niche as a use case. The Fire pet currently offers no compelling reason to buy at any level.

Most of the other spells including summoned weapons are worthwhile, buy them when they are affordable. Also practice up casting skills from infrequently used disciplines (divination, abjuration, alteration, etc) as the Elementaist levels. This will make it a little easier when needing to use one of those skills at a critical moment in higher levels. Nothing is worse than needing to use Gate in an emergency, fizzling the spell 10 times, and running out of mana in the process.

The Elementalist has a few lines of spells related specifically to fighting elementals, things like charm, special elemental damage, fear, etc. These spells are not needed or used by the vast majority of Elementalists currently. While there are some lower level elemental areas, they are not widely camped, so seldom encountered. There has never seemed to be a point in attempting to charm an elemental enemy as a pet, it clearly will not be needed up to level 50. The Elementalist will likely not invest in Charisma and this is required to have a reasonable charm length before a break. So the whole line of elemental specialty spells are currently all niche, at best.

sections.title: Pet/Elementalist Combo Spells
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: The Elementalist has a line of "blast" spells that are instant cast damage and on their own cooldown. By themselves they simply do quick damage, but if used directly after the pet successfully lands their ability, the blast spell can produce extra effects/damage. These are usually helpful combinations, however there is one that can cause trouble in a group, the Air pet's Staggering Winds in combination with the Elementalist's Blast of Fire. When this combo is triggered it converts Blast of Fire to Vortex of Fire, which is a target AoE damage spell that damages all enemies (and potentially the Elementalist if too close) in the area of effect (~5 meter radius from the target). For a group fighting several adds that are mezzed, this is a problem! So use a different blast spell, like Blast of Water to avoid the combo with the Air pet in a group. Solo, with another Elementalist, or with an Elementalist group specially set up to quad mobs, Vortex of Fire can be very handy! Note that one Elementalist's Blast line of spells work not only with their own pet, but also any other Elementalist's pet of a compatible Blast combo type.

To trigger a combo, simply cast the Blast spell directly after the pet's ability lands on the target (within a few seconds). The player can set the pet's ability to manual and trigger it themselves to gaurantee timing.
See Evil's Elementalist Guide for more on Elementalist blast spell-pet ability combos.

sections.title: Solo Tactics
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: The Elementalist is OK solo so long as they do not take on more then their pet can handle. Early on, yellow conning mobs are doable, but the Elementalist will have to act as the tank and not allow the pet to absorb all of the damage. After the early levels, things change rapidly and soloing anything conning white or above is not a good idea. Keep in mind that the pets do not level with the Elementalist. A level one pet is level one when the Elementalist is level three. A blue con mob to the Elementalist can be a yellow con mob to the pet. Pets will naturally feel very powerful every four levels and diminish somewhat as the Elementalist levels up beyond the pet.

With green con mobs (to the pet), the Air or Water pet will be able to reliably handle two, three, and even four with little trouble. Vortex of Fire with the Air pet can help here as the Elementalist can effectively quad mobs. However the targets have to be managed properly or the Elementalist will have multiple mobs leaving the pet and attacking the Elementalist. The Elementalist will need switch targets and have the pet attack each one with a few hits to gain effective aggro. When all of the attacking targets have good aggro on the pet, the Elemetalist can initiate Vortex of Fire a couple of times to burn all four down. This takes some practice, but is very effective with green conning mobs.

With a blue con mob (to the pet), an add can be a serious problem. The Earth pet is probably a better choice in the mid levels if attacking blue con mobs, albeit slower fights. White or beyond conning mobs (to the pet) are not worth the risk or the time. The Elementalist will have to dump a lot of mana to kill off the target and keep the pet alive. This results in a long downtime to heal and med up mana. An add of any kind in this situation will probably result in a dead pet and a lost fight.

One of the DPS caster hamstrings in the game is the global cooldown. This severely limits the damage output irrespective of the casting speed that the Elementalist (or really any DPS caster) can put out in a short period of time. The Elementalist does have a good one-two punch, by casting a Blast spell, which is instant with it's own cooldown, and then casting a DD spell immediately afterward.

In a solo fight with the pet on only one target, the Elementalist can opt to not really add damage, but just keep healing the pet. It is important to do something though, as merely sending the pet to attack and nothing else will result in the mob corpse disappearing and no experience gained. The corpse disappearing instantly on death may sometimes happen anyway, the behavior isn't 100% reliable as server latency can result in the server not calculating that the player did an action in time. The developers did this to prevent someone from parking a pet right on a spawn location and just letting it auto-kill, but the current implementation is hamfisted.

In a risky fight, like taking on a blue conned named or anything that is just a tough fight, a good tactic for pet healing is to sit right at the pet location where the fight is taking place. The Elementalist can use bind wound on the pet once every 60 seconds. If the pet is taking too much damage at any point, cast a pet heal, sit down again immediately, and continue medding and bind wounds on the pet when possible. Be sure to have a supply of summoned bandages on hand before the fight.

With the Water pet while fighting solo (or in a group), the Elementalist can sit and occasionally cast only a heal or one of the blast spells and sit down again quickly. For a long fight with a named mob, this can make a big difference in the outcome as the mana recovery while sitting with a Water pet is a big help in stretching the overall mana pool depletion rate. Even if the blast spells don't seem to have as good mana to damage ratio as one of the longer casting damage spells, the mana recovery from an "instant cast and sit" makes the effeciency greater than the what calcuation says.
Always try to pick up buffs for the pet before venturing if possible. Everything from SoW to AC/HP/Haste/Strength, it makes a difference and is especially noticable while solo.

sections.title: Group Tactics
sections.source: A Guide For A Starting Elementalist
lines: For most all group leveling, the Elementalist is merely siccing the pet on the main assist's target and throwing in a DD spell occasionally. Use a Blast+DD as a combo for harder targets that have a lot of HP. It's a good idea to open up with a Element Break debuff and send the pet in as a matter of regular habit, particularly when the group is attacking yellow or red conning mobs. This will help minimize wasted mana due to resists of a Blast or DD spell.

In later levels, depending on the group healing and tank situation, for example a single over-worked Druid as the group healer, the Elementalist can help out by summoning lots of bandages, for both the tank and Druid (and any other group member that needs them). The Elementalist can also regularly summon manastones for the Druid when they get really low on mana. This can help the Druid out, they use the manastones to recover mana quickly and bandage themselves while medding and not wasting their mana to regen. Don't wait to ask about this in a group! If a group member extremely low on mana, just summon the stuff up and hand it out. Sometimes summoned arrows or throwing knives are asked for, but this is pretty rare. Other pet classes and charmers in the group will often ask for weapons to give their pets, be ready with them.

The Elementalist should strive to not burn down mana too much while in the group. The pet is the main source of the Elementalist's damage output, everything else is a bonus. Keep the mana at hand for bosses and bad situations, like too many adds, or repeatedly summoning manastones for critical players that are just about out of mana. A crowd controlling Enchanter that is OOM with 4 or 5 unplanned adds he is trying to keep mezzed will thank the stars that a manastone was handed over in the middle of the bad situation.

If chaos erupts in a group, particuarly tight quarters, the Elementalist can use the pet to off-tank adds, possibly giving time for escape, via running or gating out. Try to acquire aggro on as much as possible by cycling targets, ordering the pet to attack each one, and turning on Provoke. Keep a cool head, but don't over-extend as the pet won't last long. Be ready to run or gate out, sacrificing the pet for staying alive.

If multiple Elementalists are in a group, there are some things to consider. For two, one should run the Water pet and the other the Air pet. For three or more one Water pet and the others can all run Air pets, or perhaps one Water, one Earth and others run Air. The aura's help everybody and each other's other pets in a group. Only the Fire pet is borderline useless, the other three all bring strong benefits to a group.

Be wary of moving with a pet through enemy areas. Invisibility (of any kind) can easily drop on the pet without the player noticing and potentially creating a train. Some player's will ask for the pet to be parked in a safe area, and have the player move through mobs while invisible, and then once in place use the /unstuck command to glitch the pet to the Elementalist (like a free teleport). This can work, but the pet needs to be set to passive (in case there is aggro problem) because a huge train can be created depending on the path to the player. There is no really good reason to move through a dangerous area with a pet trailing behind. It is best to simply drop the pet and recreate it when the final camp location has been set (keep a supply of Crushed Malachite on had for this).

sections.title: Level 1-8
lines: Early game enchanter mainly functions as a party buffer and an extra pair of weapon swings on mobs alongside your Shadowkin Defender Pet. Your primary focus in a group will be maintaining your buffs on your allies, casting Mesmerize on targets that your group is not currently focusing, and melee attacking the primary mob.

Torment is your only direct damage spell starting at level 1, although it does a decent amount of damage and reduces the targets stats it is very expensive to cast and draws a significant amount of threat/hate early on which can cause problems for your tank. Utilize it sparingly as a damage dealer to avoid pulling threat/hate.
Haste is a great pick up after level 4 and your melee party members will love you for it. It can also be cast on your pet as well as your allies' pets to make grinding much faster.

Placate as a spell is extremely useful and can be utilized when pulling to help break camps or split large packs of mobs. Placate in general seems to have a high chance of failing on mobs that are conning above green which can create some dangerous situations for your group so utilize it wisely and always be prepared for it to fail. (Its a great tool for sneaking past mobs that are inadvertently guarding gathering nodes such as ores)
Scintillating Shock is a cheap AoE stun which is extremely useful for setting up crowd controls and can be utilized as an interrupt.

Charm is a very versatile spell as its power will vary based on the mob charmed. Experimentation with different mob types will help you to better understand when and where it should be used. Keep in mind that any useful abilities that you will have access to from a charmed mob will also be used against you when the charm inevitably breaks.

sections.title: Level 8-15
lines: Level 8 is when Enchanter really starts to open up mainly due to the Enchant Ally spell which is an extremely enjoyable spell to use as it gives you some spells to cast regularly while smacking mobs with your allies.

Enchant Ally is a buff that can be cast on a friendly creature, either your pet if you're soloing or your tank if you're grouping. Once cast it will allow you to see through your tank's vision which can be toggled as well as providing two new spells which you can drag from the Enchant Ally window onto your hotbar in order to cast them manually. The two spells are Runeskin which will provide a small damage shield on your enchanted ally for a brief period of time, and Shadow Spike which is a decent consistent damage dealer if cast off-cooldown. Enchant Ally also offers the target some extra health.

Root is a valuable spell and you will likely find yourself swapping it in when you're grinding a pack of mobs that will warrant it's use. It is most commonly used on fast-moving fleeing mobs which risk pulling additional mobs after they begin fleeing on low health. When you notice a mob is getting low its best to preemptively cast Root before the mob begins running and then spam casting it as the damage your group is doing will potentially break the root. If you're on root duty, your primary focus should be to spam cast Root on fleeing mobs and let your group whack them until they're dead. A rooted mob that is capable of ranged attacking will still be able to do so, so mesmerizing is more beneficial for these types of mobs.
Tranquility is a must for yourself and any mana users in your party, add it to your buff rotation.

Captivate is stronger version of Mesmerize that will sleep your target for double the time and has a lower chance of breaking. It is more expensive than Mesmerize so if you find yourself struggling for mana you can always swap it out for the less reliable option.

Fascinate is your first area-of-effect Mesmerize spell and is highly situational. When things get hectic it might be beneficial to cast it on a large pack of mobs and hope your group is targeting correctly. If it works out your group will definitely pat you on the back.
Torture is the next upgrade of your torment spell, utilize it sparingly as a damage dealer as it can draw a large amount threat/hate.

sections.title: Equipment Guides
lines: Lumeira's Early Gear Path:
Welcome to Monks & Memories!
1.) Fourfold Sashes:
Your first priority as a Monk in pre-alpha is to begin your Fourfold Sash Questline.
There are currently three levels of this quest-line.

1.5.) *NOTE: The 'a strong sparring monk' and 'a tough sparring monk' NPCs for the first step of the quest line - do NOT give EXP, but they do drop gear and give no faction hit when you down them. They DO drop Tattered Cloth Armor and lowest level weapons of all types. Even Weapons monks cannot use. You can just punch them in the face and do not have to '/say spar' to fight them. They spawn quickly and are a good source of very low level gear and minor coin early on.

Sell your excess gear to the 'Used Weapons Dealer' and the 'Cloth Armor' Merchant in the Night Market district of Nights Harbor. (its name is currently just Cloth Armor). DO NOT SELL TO THE SHIFTY GNOME. He will give you 2.5x LESS than the proper merchants do.***
2.) Hammers & Bags & Boots: Addicted to Spending

After spending some time farming yourself some Silver, (if you have 100 Bronze, you have 1 silver - you do not have to convert the bronze at a bank, the merchants will do so automatically), its time to make your way to the Night Market and pick up a few things. The prices of these items changes a bit with every playtest, but expect to need around 12 Silver for everything. Or spend some time and craft them yourself.
a.) Corroded Bronze Warhammer x2 from 'Used Weapons Dealer' -- These are the best weapons you will have until you can craft/buy/loot two Steel Warhammers much later on.

b.) Small Field Pack x1, Satchel x2, Pouch x2-4 from 'Bags and Packs' (Placeholder Name). Don't bother saving up 1 gold for the Backpack. That is 100 Silver. Craft it yourself or buy from a Player if you really want it.

**OPTIONAL: Fine Cloth Boots from 'Cloth Armor' (Placeholder Name). People often craft and sell these boots to this merchant, and they have 3 AC. Your Round Kick ability deals bonus damage based on the AC of your boots. You will need as much help as you can get for the next step.
3.) Green Drakeling Scale Armor: Adventure Time!

After finishing at least your Second Degree Fourfold Sash, gotten some Cloth Armor and reached Level 4 to unlock Feign Death -- It's time to quite literally risk it all! You're a Monk, this is what we do. Get used to it.
We're going to the other side of the continent! To Keeper's Bight >> Faelindral/Evershade Weald. On a boat. I tried running once...we...we're not going to do that.

Kidding, of course, but there is a significant chance of dying. So throw all your money and gear in the Bank before making the trip. You can later retrieve all of that gear and money at the Bank in Faelindral. WARNING: Banks are no longer shared across regions.

There is a Boat that leaves the Docks of Nights Harbor at exactly 9AM GAME TIME. Type /time in game to get the game time. You will obviously want to be on that boat before it leaves, so arrive around 7AM.

From the West Gate of Nights Harbor, follow the signs that say Twilight Harbor. There are technically two harbors, one smaller and tucked away, and another much bigger and obvious harbor. Make sure you're at the bigger of the two.
The boat will sail in and dock at the middle most dock. There is another boat that does not move, that boat has barrels on it. If you see barrels, you're wrong.

KEEPER'S BIGHT: Once you are sailing, the boat will enter several zones, eventually docking at Shallow Shoals. Do not jump off here. Keep sailing until you arrive at Keeper's Bight at long last. Make sure you jump off the boat here before it leaves again at 9PM.
-- Once you have hopped off the boat, WAIT FOR DAYLIGHT. Keeper's Bight is very dangerous and very dark. You will want the sun lighting your way.

-- After hopping off the boat, you will see an alternating lift going up a high cliff. Jump onto the lift and head up into the little settlement above. Not much is here at the moment, ignore it. We are going to follow the left wall out of the settlement gate and make our way through the forest, dodging wolves that hate us every 5 seconds. Immediately Feign Death if you get aggro, and wait 10 seconds for aggro to drop and let the mob move away. You can also follow the left wall/cliff so you don't get lost.
You will eventually find the zone-line to Evershade Weald which holds the Elvish City of Faelindral in its canopy.

From here, follow the path aways until you find a platform with a few guards around it and a few other NPCS. This is the Newbie Lift. There is a Bell you can click on this platform that will bring down a lift to take you up into Faelindral. I Recommend asking for a Bind in /ooc before you explore too much. Don't wanna fall out of a tree and spawn back in Night Harbor. "/OOC Can anyone spare a bind at the Newbie Lift?".

Once you have taken the lift, you are going to spend 17 minutes getting lost before accidentally finding 'Takalea Scaletender' at the Leatherworkers / Tanners guild. I'd give you better directions but I am simply incapable of understanding tree cities. You don't need to talk to her, as her triggers are a bit unresponsive for some reason. You just need to acquire and deliver to her her the items she requires to make 4 (more planned) pieces of very strong armor.
Don't forget to grab your items from the bank before you go out exploring the forest.
More info on this armor set and quest below.
Green Drakeling Scale Armor Quest(s)
Note - for those of you who are too timid to cross the world, you can settle for the scarab armor quests which are comparable fashion, but notably worse AC for your kicks.
TO BE CONTINUED/EXPANDED

sections.title: Shaman Noobie Guide
lines: New to Shaman? Your job is to make fights safer and your group stronger. You slow enemies, weaken them, and keep healing-over-time spells on your allies. You can deal damage too, but your support spells are usually your biggest contribution.

sections.title: Your First Priorities
lines: Complete your Shaman starter quest. It introduces the class and gives you starting gear. Ask a guard or guild trainer where to find your Shaman trainer and spell vendor.
Spend most of your bonus attribute points on Wisdom, then Stamina. Wisdom helps with healing and mana; Stamina gives you more health and more room to use Consume safely.

Learn your core spells as you level. At level 1, start with Minor Spirit Mending, Berserker Spirit, and Spirit Bane. At level 4, prioritize Omen of Lethargy. Pact of Haste arrives at level 8; Consume and Pact of Renewal arrive at level 12.

sections.title: A Simple Fight Routine
lines: Before a group pull: Cast Berserker Spirit on the group and Pact of Haste on melee allies. Keep Ancestral Wisdom on yourself.

When the fight starts: Let the tank get the enemy’s attention, then cast Omen of Lethargy on the target. This is your signature slow. Slowing an enemy early can prevent more damage than healing after it has already landed. If the slow is resisted, try again.

During the fight: Keep Pact of Renewal on the tank before their health gets low. Use Spirit Mending for a quicker heal when someone needs a top-up. Add damage-over-time spells when the group is stable and you have mana to spare.

sections.title: Healing and Mana
lines: Shaman healing works best when you plan ahead. Pact of Renewal heals over time, so apply it before the tank is in trouble. Spirit Mending is your faster single-target heal. You’re a steady healer and support class, rather than a burst-heal specialist.

Consume trades health for mana and has a 45-second cooldown. Use it when you’re safe and healthy, then heal yourself over time if needed. Don’t use Consume while you’re taking hits or trying to recover from an emergency.

sections.title: Soloing
lines: For a basic solo fight, slow the enemy, apply Malady, and let your healing-over-time spell work while you attack. If the fight turns against you, use Root to make space and recover. Shamans don’t have a combat pet, so rely on your slow, damage-over-time spells, and self-healing.

sections.title: Remember This
lines: Buff before the pull. Slow early. Heal before the tank is in danger. Consume only when it’s safe.
Spell ranks and balance can change during Early Access. Check your trainer for the latest upgrades.

sections.title: How to Play a Shaman
lines: The Shaman is a support class built around making dangerous fights more manageable. You slow enemies, weaken them with Omens, keep healing-over-time spells running on allies, and improve your group with physical buffs and haste. Your damage is useful, especially in longer fights, but your first responsibility is keeping the group safe.

A Shaman’s value often shows up in what does not happen: the tank takes fewer hits, enemies are easier to finish, and the healer has more time to react. You are not expected to out-damage dedicated damage classes or replace a Cleric’s emergency healing.

sections.title: Choose Your Priorities
lines: Keep your important spells current. Buy upgrades to your slow, healing, and buffs when they become available. A spell that is several ranks behind can be less reliable or effective.

Put Wisdom first when building your character. Wisdom supports your Shaman’s casting. Stamina is a strong second choice because extra health improves your survival and gives you more room to use Consume.
Carry the utility spells you actually use. Gate, Soulbind, cures, Purge, Root, and invisibility can solve problems that another damage spell cannot.
Save mana for your job. Slow and healing should come before optional damage. If the fight is safe, use spare mana to add damage-over-time spells.

sections.title: Before a Group Pull
lines: Buff the party with Berserker Spirit, or Tribal Spirit if you have researched it and brought the required Ritual Talismans.
Put Pact of Haste on the group’s melee attackers.
Keep Ancestral Wisdom active on yourself.
Agree with the other healer who is covering the tank and who is watching the rest of the group.
Make sure you know the group’s target and can see its health bar.

sections.title: During the Fight
lines: Once the tank has the enemy’s attention, apply Omen of Lethargy. Keep Pact of Renewal on the tank before their health gets low, then use Spirit Mending for quicker top-ups. On a difficult enemy, add Omen of Enfeeblement to reduce its physical threat. Use Omen of Susceptibility when your group can benefit from lower Disease, Holy, and Magic resistance.
When the group is stable, add Malady and Ghostly Blight. Keep watching health bars while they tick. Stop casting damage spells if the tank needs healing or your mana is getting low.

sections.title: Soloing
lines: Soloing is slower and more deliberate than fighting in a group. Buff yourself, slow the enemy, apply Malady, and use Pact of Renewal or another heal-over-time spell to stay healthy while you attack. Use Omen of Enfeeblement on a tough target. If a fight turns against you, Root the enemy and create space to recover or escape.

sections.title: Mana and Recovery
lines: Consume converts your health into mana and has a 45-second cooldown. Use it when you are safe, not while an enemy is hitting you. After using it, restore your health with a heal-over-time spell or by resting before the next pull. Sitting to meditate between fights is part of managing your resources; do not feel you need to spend every point of mana on optional damage.
Shaman buffs, heals, and debuffs all compete for mana. A good Shaman chooses the spell that will help the current fight most, rather than casting every available spell on every target.

sections.title: Omen of Lethargy: Your Signature Slow
lines: Omen of Lethargy reduces an enemy’s attack speed. Because the target attacks less often, your group takes less incoming damage. Cast it after the tank has established control of the target. If the spell is resisted, try again promptly. Keep buying stronger ranks as you level: the slow line improves at levels 16, 32, and 48.

sections.title: Pact of Renewal and Spirit Mending: Healing
lines: Pact of Renewal is your main single-target heal-over-time. It works best when applied before the tank is in danger, allowing its healing to tick while the fight continues.

Spirit Mending is your short-cast direct heal. Use it when an ally needs a quicker top-up than a heal-over-time can provide. Do not wait until the tank is nearly defeated to begin healing; prevention is safer and usually more efficient than trying to recover from a large health loss.
Rite of Mending heals the group over time and has a longer cooldown. Save it for difficult fights or moments when several party members are taking damage. The group-heal line begins at level 20.

sections.title: The Three Omens: Debuffing Enemies
lines: Omen of Lethargy reduces attack speed. Use it on the group’s main target in nearly every serious fight.
Omen of Enfeeblement lowers Strength, Dexterity, and Agility. It is valuable against dangerous physical enemies, especially when your group needs to reduce incoming damage.
Omen of Susceptibility lowers Disease, Holy, and Magic resistance. It helps your own damage spells and can support other casters. Use it when the fight will last long enough for the group to benefit.
For ordinary enemies, prioritize the slow. Add the other Omens when the target is dangerous or your group can take advantage of the extra debuffs.

sections.title: Berserker Spirit, Tribal Spirit, and Pact of Haste
lines: Berserker Spirit increases physical attributes and is a useful group buff. Tribal Spirit is its group-focused researched counterpart; it requires a Ritual Talisman each time you cast it. Pact of Haste increases melee attack speed, so prioritize it on allies who deal most of their damage through weapon attacks.
Buffs take time and mana to maintain. Refresh the important ones before a pull or when there is a safe pause, rather than interrupting an urgent heal to refresh a minor buff.

sections.title: Consume: Trading Health for Mana
lines: Consume restores mana at the cost of your health. It is an important part of the Shaman’s resource kit, but the 45-second cooldown means timing matters. Use it while safe and healthy, then heal yourself or rest before taking another dangerous pull. Avoid using it when you are tanking, taking damage, or likely to need an emergency heal.

sections.title: Malady, Ghostly Blight, and Spirit Bane: Damage
lines: Malady deals Disease damage over time.
Ghostly Blight deals Magic damage over time.
Spirit Bane is your direct Magic damage line.

Damage spells are best used after you have handled the group’s immediate needs. On a long fight, apply your damage-over-time spells and then return your attention to healing and debuffing. Omen of Susceptibility can make Disease and Magic damage more effective against the target.

sections.title: Root, Cures, Purge, and Escape
lines: Root holds a target in place and can give you room to escape a bad solo pull. Purge removes a beneficial effect from an enemy. Cure Disease, Cure Poison, and Dispel Magic remove harmful effects from allies; use the matching cure when someone is affected. At level 40, Ritual of Escape can help the entire group disengage and recover. It has a long cooldown, so treat it as an emergency tool.

sections.title: Level Specific Guides
lines: Shaman spells are learned in ranks. Visit your trainer when you reach a new spell level, and prioritize upgrades to your slow and healing before buying every damage spell. Some important group spells are researched rather than sold by a vendor.

sections.title: Levels 1–3: Learn the Basics
lines: Minor Spirit Mending: Your starting single-target heal.
Berserker Spirit: A physical-stat buff for your group.
Spirit Bane: Your direct-damage spell.
Polar Align: North: A utility spell to keep available as needed.
At these levels, practice targeting the tank, healing before health becomes critical, and keeping your group buffed. Do not spend all your mana on Spirit Bane if you may need it to heal.

sections.title: Levels 4–7: Get Your Slow
lines: Level 4 is a major Shaman milestone. Buy Omen of Lethargy as soon as possible; it is your signature slow and one of the most valuable spells you bring to a group. Also look for Lesser Spirit Mending, Malady, Ancestral Wisdom, Gate, Soulbind, Spirit Bane II, and Summon Drink.
If you cannot afford every spell, prioritize the slow and healing upgrades first, then buy utility and damage spells as your money allows.

sections.title: Levels 8–11: Buff the Melee
lines: At level 8, learn Pact of Haste and the stronger Spirit Mending rank. Other useful spells include Minor Regeneration, Greater Malady, Purge, Speed of the Wild, Invisibility versus Undead, and Summon Food.
Before a group pull, apply Pact of Haste to melee allies. Keep your slow current and continue using Malady when the group is stable.

sections.title: Levels 12–15: Add Your Main Heal-over-Time
lines: At level 12, learn Consume and Pact of Renewal . Pact of Renewal becomes your key proactive tank heal. You also gain Omen of Enfeeblement, Ghostly Blight, Root, Cure Disease, and Dispel Magic.

This is a good level range to start using the full Shaman routine: slow the target, keep Pact of Renewal on the tank, debuff dangerous enemies, and add damage-over-time spells when safe. Use Consume only when your health and the situation allow it.

sections.title: Levels 16–19: Upgrade the Slow and Add the Third Omen
lines: At level 16, purchase Greater Omen of Lethargy . This improves the slow to 20 percent and is one of the most important upgrades for your group. You also gain Greater Pact of Haste, Berserker Rage, Omen of Susceptibility, Sickness, Ancestral Wisdom II, Invisibility, and Cure Poison.
Use Omen of Susceptibility when your damage-over-time spells or your group’s casters can benefit from lowered resistances. Keep using Omen of Lethargy as your first priority on dangerous targets.

sections.title: Levels 20–23: Group Healing
lines: At level 20, you gain your first group heal, Lesser Rite of Mending , along with Greater Pact of Renewal, Greater Spirit Mending, Lesser Regeneration, and Spirit Blight.
Rite of Mending affects the party and has a longer cooldown. Save it for encounters where several people are taking damage rather than using it as a routine heal on every pull.

sections.title: Levels 24–27: Upgrade Debuffs and Control
lines: At level 24, upgrade Consume and all three Omens. You also gain Curing Ritual, Ghostly Miasma, Greater Sickness, and Lurching Impairment. These spells improve your ability to sustain mana, weaken difficult enemies, cure disease across the group, and control a dangerous target.
For a routine fight, the slow may be enough. For a named enemy or a difficult camp, add Enfeeblement and Susceptibility when your group has the time and mana to benefit.

sections.title: Level 28 and Beyond: Keep Your Core Lines Current
lines: At level 28, look for Pact of Restoration, Rite of Mending, Ancestral Wisdom III, and Greater Purge. After level 28, continue prioritizing stronger slows, haste, healing, and Omens. Add damage upgrades after your support spells are current. Research Tribal Spirit and Communion of Regeneration when you have access to them; they are not ordinary vendor purchases.

sections.title: Zone Specific Guides
lines: Your race determines which starting areas are available to you. Begin with your local Shaman starter quest, learn the nearby routes, and ask a guard or guild trainer where to find your class trainer and spell vendor. The level ranges below are starting recommendations, not strict rules; group size, gear, and the enemies you encounter all affect difficulty.

sections.title: Faelindral and Evershade Weald
lines: Faelindral is a Wood Elf starting area. Complete the local starter quests and use the nearby low-level enemies to learn your spells before moving farther into the Weald. Around levels 4–9, the scout paths in Evershade Weald offer wolves and orc scouts. Shamans can contribute strongly here by slowing the kill target and keeping a heal-over-time on the tank.
Mossbound Aelurath in Evershade Weald is also a potential target for the Heartwood Circlet of the Warden. Check the area and your group’s level before engaging named enemies.

sections.title: Night Harbor
lines: Night Harbor is a starting option for Humans and Ogres, and also an option for Wood Elves. The newbie yards near the gates are appropriate for levels 1–5. Follow the Shaman starter quest and ask local guards for directions to the trainer and spell vendor. Errol Shrewtender is the Shaman guildmaster associated with Night Harbor.
Night Harbor is also a useful place to check for early gear and spells. Before traveling elsewhere, make sure you have the latest slow and healing spells you can afford.

sections.title: Underdocks
lines: Underdocks is a starting area for Goblins, Ogres, and Deep Gnomes. The newbie yard is suitable for early levels; the nearby Deepcut Bandit Camp offers another option around levels 5–6 and connects with bounty quests.

From roughly levels 7–12, the Wererat Warrens are a possible leveling area. Wererats can spread disease, so Cure Disease becomes useful once you learn it at level 12. Bring food and drink, keep your escape spell available, and avoid pulling multiple enemies until you know how quickly you can control them. Elderbones and Ghouls are also viable in this bracket. The plagued Mycelial cave also has great exp but has less room for multiple groups.

sections.title: Early Group Dungeons and Camps
lines: Tomb of the Last Wyrmsbane, levels 3–11: An early group dungeon where your slow and melee buffs can help each pull go more smoothly. Join a group and follow its pull pace; do not run ahead to tag enemies.
Infested Crypt, levels 8–14: The area near the entrance offers easier solo pulls, with spider broods deeper inside. Move farther in only when you are comfortable handling the increased risk.
Tel Ekir, levels 10–15: Ashira camps provide group opportunities and possible Wisdom-focused equipment. Go with a group if you are unsure of the camp’s difficulty.
Fallen Pass and Keeper’s Bight, levels 18–27: These areas offer denser group camps and several useful chain-armor drops. Keep your slow and healing ranks current before joining a camp.

Before entering a dungeon, agree on who is pulling, what the kill target is, and who is responsible for emergency healing. A Shaman’s slow is valuable, but it works best when the group attacks one controlled target at a time.

sections.title: What to Look For
lines: Shamans wear chain armor. When comparing gear, prioritize Wisdom, then Stamina and mana. Stamina is especially useful because more health helps you survive and gives you more room to use Consume. Armor and hit points are also valuable when you expect to fight close to enemies.

For weapons, look for a blunt or piercing weapon that supports your stats. A weapon with Wisdom, Stamina, or mana can be a better choice for group play than one with only higher damage. A Wisdom off-hand item is also a strong option when available.

sections.title: Early Items to Watch For
lines: Awakened Spirit Pouch: A starter-quest reward in Night Harbor. It provides Strength, Stamina, Wisdom, health, and mana.
Ward of Wisdom: An early secondary item sold by Aide Aida in Night Harbor, with Wisdom and defensive stats.
Amulet of Wisdom: A Wisdom and mana option sold by Aide Aida in Night Harbor.
Heartwood Circlet of the Warden: A head item with Wisdom, Stamina, health, and mana. It drops from Mossbound Aelurath in Evershade Weald.
Staff of Spores: A Wisdom-bearing weapon associated with the “Mushroom Menace” quest in Faelindral.
Alchemist’s Mail Hood and Shawl of the Font Seeress: Wisdom-focused pieces available from enemies in Tel Ekir.
Maul of the Wise: A Wisdom and mana weapon associated with Najm the Mirage in Tel Ekir.

sections.title: Later Upgrades
lines: As you move into higher-level group areas, look for chain armor that combines Wisdom with Stamina, health, or mana. The Shaman guide lists options such as Stillbrook Coif, Chainfall Gauntlets, Zirat’s Blackwire Cuff, and Boulderstride Chain Greaves in the Fallen Pass and Keeper’s Bight areas.

These are targets, not a required set. Do not delay leveling because you are missing one specific drop. Replace gear when the new item is a real improvement to your Wisdom, survivability, mana, or armor.

sections.title: Buying and Comparing Gear
lines: Check whether the item improves Wisdom, Stamina, mana, health, or armor.
Compare the full item, not just one stat. A small Wisdom gain may not be worth losing a large amount of health or armor.
Ask your group whether a drop is useful to another class before claiming it.
Use the item database to confirm current stats and drop locations; item values and availability can change during Early Access.
